row.note: The commentary's jailed dreamer presses the future drink and later serves his master; in his own dream the cupbearer squeezes grapes into Pharaoh's cup, making the pressed product and its hoped-for release concrete.
The commentary links the pressing dream to escape from custody; Joseph predicts that the cupbearer will regain his office in three days and put the cup in Pharaoh's hand.
The commentary's rescued prisoner is asked to mention Joseph to his master; Joseph asks the cupbearer to remember him and bring him out of this house, joining another man's release to his own wait.
The commentary makes forgotten remembrance prolong confinement; Genesis says the restored cupbearer did not remember Joseph but forgot him.
The commentary's prison years stretch after the cupbearer's release; Genesis opens Pharaoh's dream after two full years, locating the delay precisely.

row.basis: seven full ears in Pharaoh's dream
row.note: The commentary notes the king's green ears as a measure of coming plenty; Genesis describes seven healthy full ears on one stalk in his dream.
The commentary opposes green and dry ears before famine; Genesis adds seven thin ears scorched by the east wind, making crop loss visible before interpretation.
The commentary's grain is kept within its covering for hard years; Joseph orders food gathered under Pharaoh's authority and stored in cities during the good years.
The commentary links sheltered grain to survival through seven severe years; Joseph explicitly says the stored food will keep the land from perishing in famine.

row.basis: ص ب ر / צבר; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary links the surah's patience to stored grain in Joseph's years; Genesis uses צבר of Joseph heaping grain like sea sand, a striking consonantal meeting that speaks of accumulation rather than proving a patience cognate.
The commentary arranges pressing and storage on a calendar; Genesis marks the completion of the seven plentiful years before the scarcity.
The commentary's hard years consume earlier stores; Genesis states the seven famine years began and Egypt still had bread, showing what advance keeping achieved.

row.basis: ع ص ر / עצר; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary pairs a held cloud with released water and dry residue; Job says God restrains waters so they dry up and sends them so they overturn earth, giving the Hebrew root an explicit hold and release contrast.

row.basis: ع ص ر / עצר; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's squeezed cloud yields rain and crops; Deuteronomy says heaven will be restrained with no rain and the land will not yield, the same root's withholding set against that fertile sequence.

row.basis: ع ص ر / עצר; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary hears rain in a pressed cloud; Solomon's prayer names heaven being shut up, using עצר, and a resulting lack of rain, clarifying how restraint can deny the expected flow.

row.basis: ع ص ر / עצר; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary lets restraint become shelter and communal response to loss; Joel orders a solemn assembly, עצרה, amid devastated crops and summoned elders, moving the root from closure to gathered supplication.

row.basis: ع ص ر / עצר; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's asr marks a day's edge and a holding together; the eighth day after seven festival days is called עצרת, a sacred closing assembly, supplying a calendrical communal use of the Hebrew root.

row.basis: ع ص ر / עצר; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's restraint can hold something within at a life threshold; Genesis says the LORD had closed every womb in Abimelech's house, using עצר for a concrete bodily closure.

row.basis: ع ص ر / עצר; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary contrasts protecting what is held with letting life emerge; Isaiah asks whether God would bring a woman to birth and then shut the womb, using עצר at the threshold of release.

The commentary connects pressing equipment and keeping grain safe in danger; Gideon threshes wheat in a winepress to hide it from Midian, joining press, harvest, and protective enclosure in one scene.
The commentary opposes a pressed hand that gives to a hand that retains everything; the proverb says one scatters and gains while one withholds what is due and comes to want.
The commentary makes released liquid an image of benefaction; the generous person in the proverb prospers and the one who waters others is watered, tying an outward flow to replenishment.
The commentary's garden owners keep produce from a poor person; Deuteronomy forbids hardening the heart or shutting the hand against a poor kinsman, identifying the hand's closure as the moral fault.
The commentary asks whether the hand's pressure releases anything; Deuteronomy commands opening the hand and lending enough to the needy, a precise ethical opposite to withholding the crop.
The commentary hears a day's diminishing time and its due wage; Leviticus forbids keeping a hired worker's pay overnight, fixing giving to the day's boundary.
The commentary's late hour and daily wage converge in the command to pay a poor hired worker that very day before sunset because he depends on the wage.
The commentary lets a long age contract to one part of a day when viewed from its end; the psalm likens a thousand years before God to yesterday once past or a watch in the night.
The commentary asks what may still be done in the short remaining span; the psalm asks to be taught to count days so the heart gains wisdom, turning elapsed time into conduct.
The commentary hears waning afternoon light as a mortal life near its end; the psalmist says his days are like an evening shadow and he withers like grass.
The commentary's afternoon is the edge before action becomes too late; attackers in Jeremiah urge an assault at noon, then lament the declining day and stretching evening shadows.
The commentary joins shrinking daylight to unfinished righteous action; Jesus says work must be done while it is day because night comes when no one can work.
The commentary treats afternoon as late opportunity with wages still in view; the vineyard owner finds laborers standing idle at the eleventh hour and asks why they have worked none of the day.
The commentary places the day's wage at the closing edge of time; at evening the vineyard owner orders the steward to call workers and pay them, beginning with the last.

row.basis: one late hour versus full day
row.note: The commentary lets an hour and an age occupy the same moral horizon; early laborers protest that the late arrivals worked one hour yet received the same payment as those bearing the day's heat.

row.basis: stored harvest and life ending tonight
row.note: The commentary's old garden owner can lose accumulated yield when time closes; God tells the man with stores for many years that his life is required tonight and asks who will possess his prepared goods.
The commentary asks whether sheltered produce is kept for wise survival or hoarded; the rich man decides to tear down barns and build bigger ones for his grain and goods.
The commentary contrasts productive giving with merely retaining a harvest; Jesus closes the barn parable by naming treasure amassed for oneself without being rich toward God.

The commentary's compression may make a gift flow; Jesus commands giving and promises a measure pressed down, shaken together, and running over into the giver's lap, explicitly joining pressure and generosity.
The commentary pairs retained produce with refusal to give what is owed; James says wages withheld from workers who harvested fields cry out, making the tight hand a charge against the landowner.
The commentary calls time a capital in which business and gain can occur; James quotes merchants planning to spend a year in a city and make a profit, before challenging their control of that span.
The commentary's long life collapses to a moment at the end; James says traders do not know tomorrow and their life appears briefly like vapor before vanishing.
The commentary's accumulated garden can be lost suddenly at life's late hour; Revelation's merchants and sailors see a wealthy city's riches laid waste in one hour.

The commentary opens with a temporal object of oath before announcing loss; Revelation's angel swears by the eternal creator that there will be no further delay, making time and impending judgment the oath's matter.
The commentary places an oath at the threshold of an end whose timing matters; Daniel sees the linen-clad figure swear by the eternal one and give a measured period until the events are finished.
The commentary includes the prayer named for asr and the day's late edge; Isaac goes out to meditate in the field toward evening, the verse later used to anchor afternoon prayer.

row.basis: Isaac's evening meditation as afternoon prayer
row.note: The commentary names salat al-asr beside the late part of the day; the rabbinic discussion reads Isaac's field meditation in Genesis 24:63 as instituting the afternoon prayer, sharpening the prayer-time comparison.
The commentary places worship at the paired ends of day and at asr; the psalmist prays evening, morning, and noon, placing the same three temporal stations around an appeal for help.
The commentary notes worship at the late-day asr hour; Peter and John go to the temple at the ninth hour, explicitly called an hour of prayer.

row.basis: fruit in its season beside water
row.note: The commentary makes time either release nourishing yield or leave dry residue; the righteous tree planted by streams bears fruit in its season and keeps its leaf from withering.
The commentary's spent, dry remainder is vulnerable to the whirlwind; the psalm compares the wicked to chaff driven away by wind, opposite the rooted fruiting tree of its preceding verse.
The commentary's fruitful garden meets destructive wind after growth; Ezekiel's lament has a vine uprooted, cast down, and dried by the east wind so its strong branches are broken.
The commentary's storm bears fire into a vineyard and removes future produce; Ezekiel has fire go out from the vine's own branch and consume its fruit, a related but differently caused loss.
The commentary joins grapes awaiting pressing to the prospect that accumulated work fails; Isaiah's vineyard has a built wine vat but yields wild grapes instead of the expected harvest.
The commentary joins shelter to a garden's exposure at the wrong moment; Isaiah announces removal of the vineyard hedge and wall, after which it will be eaten and trampled.
The commentary's pressed cloud should bring rain to grain and garden; Isaiah commands clouds not to rain on the failed vineyard, turning off the source of yield.

The commentary's old owner has vulnerable children when sudden wind destroys provision; in Job's report a great desert wind strikes the house, killing his children, giving the family vulnerability a narrative parallel.
The commentary's shelter encloses a stretch of time; the manslayer must stay in the city of refuge until the high priest dies, making protection and a measured period inseparable.

row.basis: ark shut around those escaping disaster
row.note: The commentary's shelter holds vulnerable lives while outside time turns dangerous; God shuts Noah into the ark after the creatures enter, a protective closure rather than a prison.

row.basis: one day and a thousand years
row.note: The commentary's cave sleepers treat centuries as part of a day; 2 Peter says with the Lord one day is like a thousand years and a thousand years like one day, offering a theological version of that scale change.

row.basis: fragrance fills a space after anointing
row.note: The commentary's perfumed passer leaves an expanding scent; Mary anoints Jesus' feet and the house fills with perfume, making the diffusion of fragrance a visible effect of a person's act.

The commentary contrasts storm dust with sweet scent lifted after a person; the beloved calls north and south winds to blow on her garden so its spices flow outward, joining moving air to fragrant release.

The commentary allows a person to leave a sweet trace rather than destructive dust; Paul says God makes the fragrance of knowing Christ perceptible through his messengers in every place, an ethical use of spreading scent.

row.basis: act before the place without work
row.note: The commentary says unperformed good becomes impossible after the remaining hour closes; Ecclesiastes urges doing what the hand finds with strength because there is no work in Sheol.

row.basis: mutual counsel while it is Today
row.note: The commentary's final surah verse makes the spared group counsel one another in a limited span; Hebrews commands daily mutual exhortation as long as it is called Today, before hearts harden.
The commentary joins reciprocal counsel to approaching closure of time; Hebrews urges meeting and encouraging one another all the more as the Day draws near.

row.basis: life's seventy or eighty years pass quickly
row.note: The commentary makes an age also an afternoon of human life; the psalm counts typical years and says even their proud part is toil and trouble before they swiftly pass.
The commentary treats one's duration as allotted time that cannot be recovered; Job says human days and months are determined and their boundary cannot be crossed.
The commentary combines late life with the day's wage; Job asks that a mortal be left alone until he completes his day like a hired worker, making the life/day analogy explicit.
The commentary's closing daylight stands for a dwindling lifetime; the psalm says a person's days pass like a shadow, a compact analogue to the age/afternoon pairing.
The commentary's old age leaves little time for unperformed action; Ecclesiastes tells the young to remember their creator before the difficult days of age arrive.

row.basis: light darkens and clouds return in old age
row.note: The commentary fuses waning light, cloud, and life's evening; Ecclesiastes' old-age poem describes darkening sun and returning clouds, reusing weather for life's close.
The commentary's closing daylight can compress unexpectedly; Amos announces that God will make the sun go down at noon, a reversal in which the day's end arrives before its expected hour.

The commentary's oath leads to a verdict about loss and good action; Amos has the LORD swear never to forget the merchants' deeds after their wish to cheat the poor, linking sworn speech to a moral reckoning.
The commentary makes a long lifetime feel like a small measure; the psalmist says God made his days handbreadths and his lifetime like nothing before God.

row.basis: ص ب ر / צבר; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary contrasts storing resources for survival with loss at life's end; the psalm uses צבר of a person heaping wealth without knowing who will gather it, a Hebrew consonantal analogue to stored capital, not an established cognate of Arabic patience.

row.basis: ص ب ر / צבר; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's lifetime of accumulated yield can disappear; Job uses צבר of a wicked man heaping silver like dust before another receives it, giving the table root a precarious accumulation scene.
The commentary's grasp can either release benefit or retain it; Proverbs forbids withholding good from one owed it when the giver has power to act.
The commentary's late hour makes deferred generosity hazardous; Proverbs forbids telling a neighbor to return tomorrow for something already in one's possession.
The commentary joins a released store to rain and overflowing gain; Malachi tells worshipers to bring the full tithe into the storehouse and promises opened windows of heaven with blessing.

The commentary asks whether a held resource becomes benefaction and later yield; Paul says sparing sowing reaps sparingly and bountiful sowing reaps bountifully, giving the hand's release a harvest consequence.

row.basis: seed and bread become fruit of generosity
row.note: The commentary connects rain-fed grain and giving; Paul says God supplies seed to the sower and bread for food and will increase the harvest of the community's righteousness.
The commentary's squeezed essence becomes generosity when it leaves the hand; Paul says enrichment should produce generosity that becomes thanksgiving to God.
The commentary's protected grain and watered garden survive time; Isaiah's LORD says he waters and guards his vineyard at every moment, a positive inverse to the lost garden.
The commentary's garden is destroyed precisely when its old owner cannot start again; the righteous in this psalm still bear fruit in old age, an explicit alternative to late-life barrenness.
The commentary makes cloud pressure lead at last to rain after withholding; Elijah's servant sees a small cloud rise from the sea as the awaited sign of rain.
The commentary's cloud, wind, and downpour may make a life-giving sequence; in Elijah's story sky darkens with clouds and wind and a heavy rain follows the drought.
The commentary's cloud may cease to release its contents; Genesis says the rain from heaven was restrained when the flood's waters began to recede, a noncognate wording of holding back rain.

row.basis: wind in fists and water in a garment
row.note: The commentary imagines grasping and containing fluid or wind before release; the riddle asks who has gathered wind in fists and bound waters in a garment, sharpening the containment image without using the table root.

The commentary juxtaposes juice extracted by pressure with a dry thirsty mouth; Job describes oppressed laborers treading winepresses yet suffering thirst, a concrete ethical reversal of access to the product.

row.basis: winepress yields red juice under feet
row.note: The commentary names pressing as extraction that can turn morally dark; Isaiah's speaker treads a winepress alone, with red liquid on his garments as an image of judgment rather than bounty.
The commentary's pressure yields liquid while approaching an end; Revelation's winepress is trodden outside the city and blood flows from it, a severe alternative to beneficial juice.
The commentary says pressing resumes after the years of shortage; Amos promises such abundance that grape treading overlaps with sowing, putting the renewed press on a compressed calendar.
The commentary's future year of squeezing marks relief; Isaiah's lament removes joy from fruitful fields and silences wine in the presses, a specific reversal of that hoped-for sound.
The commentary distinguishes protective storage from hoarding that destroys the gift; people keep manna until morning against instruction and it breeds worms and stinks.
The commentary's grain kept through scarcity makes restraint beneficial; the double portion of manna saved for the Sabbath does not stink or breed worms, showing a purposeful period of keeping.
The commentary's kinship can function as a human refuge; Naomi identifies Boaz as a near relative and one of their redeemers, giving the abstract family shelter a named agent.
The commentary's distressed person grasps a shelter; Boaz blesses Ruth for coming to take refuge under the LORD's wings, making reliance on protection explicit.
The commentary's encircling armor is linked to rescue; Isaiah depicts the LORD wearing righteousness as a breastplate and salvation as a helmet, giving protective equipment a moral meaning.
The commentary's armor encloses a threatened body and its storm carries fire; Ephesians tells believers to take a shield able to quench flaming darts, making protective gear meet fire directly.
The commentary's harvest may be erased by a violent wind; Hosea says sowing wind reaps whirlwind and yields no grain, coupling failed crop and intensified storm.

row.basis: chaff and dust swept by storm
row.note: The commentary's whirlwind lifts and scatters dry residue; Isaiah likens nations driven away to mountain chaff before wind and whirling dust before storm.
The commentary sees wind raise dust into a moving trace; Nahum depicts the LORD's path in whirlwind and storm and clouds as dust of his feet, recasting the atmospheric image as divine approach.

The commentary says a passing person's fragrant trace can remain rather than dust; Paul calls his community the aroma of Christ among those being saved and those perishing, specifying the trace's different reception.

The commentary pairs a spreading scent with a good trace after someone passes; Jesus says the woman's anointing act will be told in her memory wherever the gospel is preached, extending the perfume scene into lasting remembrance.
The commentary lets pressure either extract a good outcome or leave dry loss; Paul describes himself as afflicted on every side yet not crushed, a distinct survival under compression.
The commentary asks what an allotted time draws out of a person; Paul says temporary affliction produces an eternal weight of glory, making brief pressure yield something lasting.
The commentary's dry remainder and burned garden represent loss after failed yield; Jesus says a branch not remaining in him withers, is gathered, and is burned.
The commentary places righteous deeds where time might produce an essence; Jesus says bearing much fruit glorifies the Father and identifies disciples, translating orchard yield into conduct.

The commentary considers a father's claim over a child's property and land kept within kinship; Naboth refuses Ahab his vineyard because it is his fathers' inheritance, showing protective refusal rather than mere stinginess.

The commentary's daughter at a life threshold can be sheltered or denied property by family control; God rules that Zelophehad's daughters receive their father's inheritance, a legal counterweight to withholding a child's share.

row.basis: ع ص ر / עצר; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's held-back life at a young woman's bodily threshold has a Hebrew counterpart when Sarai says the LORD has restrained her from bearing children, using עצר for barred fertility.

row.basis: ع ص ر / עצר; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary gives asr the sense of being kept for a period, as with Joseph in custody; Doeg is described as detained before the LORD at Nob, an actual Hebrew use of עצר for a person's enforced stay.

row.basis: ع ص ر / עצר; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's cloud can be held so the land dries rather than receiving its yield; God says if he restrains the heavens so there is no rain, communal repentance is needed, using עצר for the adverse closure.

row.basis: ع ص ر / עצר; table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's threatened garden and common counsel meet in Joel's call to consecrate a fast and summon an עצרה, a gathered assembly facing devastation rather than a private refuge.

row.basis: wind cannot be held; death day unavoidable
row.note: The commentary connects grasping wind with a narrowing life; Ecclesiastes says no one can confine the wind or rule the day of death, reversing imagined human control over either.
The commentary's husk and cave both hold what must survive a dangerous stretch; Noah is told to build an ark with rooms and cover it with pitch, a deliberately sealed shelter.

The commentary's refuge can enclose what feels like one interval but lasts a long span; Genesis dates the drying earth in Noah's six hundred and first year, after the ark kept its occupants through the flood.
The commentary hears time as capital that may produce a return; the master says the servant could at least have deposited entrusted money with bankers to collect it with interest.
The commentary's closed hand may end with nothing retained; the talents parable says what the one with nothing has will be taken, following the buried and unproductive entrusted sum.
The commentary's allotted span is time for productive action; the nobleman entrusts money to servants and tells them to do business until he comes back.
The commentary urges righteous work before late daylight ends; Ephesians asks readers to make the most of the time because the days are evil, relating available time to conduct.
The commentary's press and stored seed reward patient good work only after waiting; Paul says not to tire of doing good because a harvest comes in due season if one does not give up.
The commentary's shrinking remainder gives urgency to generosity; Paul says while there is opportunity the community should do good to everyone, especially its own household.
The commentary's age ends like spent vegetation; 1 Peter says human glory falls like grass's flower after quoting Isaiah, making impermanence the context for the lasting word in the next verse.

row.basis: short day, much work, wage, pressing master
row.note: The commentary hears asr as late working time with a day's pay; Rabbi Tarfon says the day is short, work abundant, workers sluggish, wage great, and master pressing, gathering its work and time images in a single teaching.
The commentary makes the last available time a chance for good action; Rabbi Tarfon adds that one need not finish the work but is not free to desist, qualifying how urgency should be heard.
The commentary makes time and deeds resemble capital and transaction; Akiva's shop parable describes extended credit, an open ledger, daily collectors, and an eventual reckoning.

The commentary treats the prison years as a bounded delay before rescue; this midrash applies Job's phrase about setting an end to darkness to Joseph's confinement, interpreting his release as arriving at its allotted time.

row.ref: Gregory of Tours, Glory of the Martyrs 94
row.basis: Ephesus sleepers' cave and long sleep
row.note: The commentary's youths find refuge in a cave and wake after centuries thinking little time has passed; Gregory retells the Christian Ephesus sleepers who are enclosed through a long sleep and later awakened, the close story behind this time-and-shelter meeting.

row.basis: Mary at puberty moved from sanctuary
row.note: The commentary's protected maiden is held at first maturity because of a boundary around her; the priests in this story worry that twelve-year-old Mary is reaching an age at which her presence may defile the sanctuary and arrange her departure, another threshold managed by enclosure.

The commentary turns a long period into a fleeting instant when viewed late; Job compares his days to a shuttle that moves quickly and ends without hope, though its textile image differs from afternoon light.
The commentary's fiery storm makes accumulated provision disappear suddenly; Proverbs says the wicked is no more when a whirlwind passes, a compact moral use of a destructive gust without a garden.

The commentary stresses that Joseph is imprisoned after his innocence becomes clear; Joseph tells the cupbearer he was taken from his land and has done nothing deserving the dungeon, making the imposed wait an injustice in his own account.
The commentary follows the dreamer whose pressed grapes precede release; Joseph gives the other prisoner a three-day prediction of execution, so the shared prison interval leads to opposite ends.

row.basis: Joseph brought out of the pit
row.note: The commentary's delayed prison years finally end in rescue; Pharaoh summons Joseph and he is hurried out of the dungeon, marking the actual release after the forgotten request.

The commentary makes the sheltered harvest available after the hard years begin and hears asr as gain; people from all lands come to Egypt to buy grain from Joseph because famine spreads, making storage a wider rescue and transaction.

The commentary lays Joseph's release and stored crop across a measured calendar; Joseph tells his brothers that two famine years have passed and five remain without plowing or harvest, specifying the continuing span that stored grain must cover.

row.basis: wages placed in a bag with holes
row.note: The commentary's time is capital and pressing separates valuable flow from residue; Haggai says people sow much but harvest little and earn wages only to put them in a pierced bag, an exact image of labor's yield leaking away.

The commentary reads the ruined garden as a picture of moral loss after withheld good; Isaiah identifies the vineyard as Israel and says God expected justice but found bloodshed, giving the garden's failed crop its ethical referent.

row.basis: blessing remains inside a grape cluster
row.note: The commentary separates extracted good from dry remainder and makes rescue an exception to loss; Isaiah says not to destroy a cluster because new wine is found in it and uses that reason to spare some servants.

The commentary's generous hand, guarded harvest, and endangered garden meet here; after the tithe promise, God says he will rebuke the devourer so crops are not destroyed and the vine does not fail to bear.

The commentary makes rain or its restraint determine whether stored effort yields food; God says he withheld rain three months before harvest and sent it on one city but not another, joining timed scarcity and uneven release.
The commentary's pressed cloud behaves like a container whose water is released; God's question about who can tip the water jars of the heavens supplies another concrete vessel image for rainfall.

The commentary contrasts released water with compressed dry residue; Job's next question describes dust hardening into a mass and clods sticking together, the arid earth after the heavenly jars image.

The commentary traces squeezed cloud to grain, plant, and provision; Isaiah says rain and snow water earth, make it sprout, and give seed to the sower and bread to the eater, a full agricultural sequence.

The commentary contrasts withholding with a pressured hand that gives; Elijah tells the widow with a final meal in view to first make him a small cake, making her scarce provision the test of release.

row.basis: flour and oil survive the drought
row.note: The commentary's protected contents last through lean time after a gift; the widow's flour jar does not empty and her oil jug does not run dry, just as Elijah had promised.

The commentary joins enclosure to a beneficial outflow rather than mere retention; Elisha tells the widow to close the door behind her and her sons and pour her small supply of oil into gathered vessels.

row.basis: sell oil, pay debt, live on remainder
row.note: The commentary hears squeezing and stored yield as income that can rescue a household; Elisha tells the widow to sell the multiplied oil, discharge her debt, and live with her sons on what remains.

row.basis: winepress yield given to freed servant
row.note: The commentary's press product becomes a gift when the hand releases it; Deuteronomy commands an owner freeing a servant to provide generously from flock, threshing floor, and winepress.

row.basis: cloak returned by sunset as shelter
row.note: The commentary pairs the day's closing edge with whether one holds back another's protection; the creditor must return a poor person's pledged cloak by sunset so that person can sleep in it.

row.basis: heaven and earth hear before verdict
row.note: The commentary's opening oath suspends its judgment until the next line; Moses first summons heaven and earth to hear his speech before his song states God's ways and Israel's response, another cosmic opening that makes the following verdict weighty.

row.basis: persecuted people seek wilderness hiding places
row.note: The commentary's youths withdraw from hostile worship to a hidden refuge; royal officers learn that Jewish families who rejected the king's command have fled to wilderness hiding places, giving flight and shelter a similar social cause.

The commentary's hidden refuge protects faithful youths across a long interval; the fugitives in 1 Maccabees die with their families when attacked on the Sabbath, a pointed reversal of safety after flight.

row.basis: open to receive, shut to repay
row.note: The commentary's grasp can receive while refusing to release; Sirach warns against stretching the hand out to take and closing it when repayment is due, exactly distinguishing the two directions of a hand.

row.basis: alms stored for a day of need
row.note: The commentary's productive gift and future shelter meet when Tobit says almsgiving stores a good treasure against a day of necessity, making generosity a reserve rather than depletion.

row.basis: hands open to receive, closed to give
row.note: The commentary's asr images make grasping ethically double; the Didache forbids extending the hands to receive while drawing them back when it is time to give, making the hand's direction the whole contrast.
The commentary names taking back a previous gift as a form of squeezing; the Didache tells hearers to give to those who ask and not demand it back, an exact ethical opposite to reclaimed donation.

The commentary reads a barren or lost garden against the time left to work; the vineyard owner has sought fruit from his fig tree for three years and orders it cut down, measuring unproductive time before loss.

The commentary's late afternoon may still allow a final productive interval; the gardener asks to leave the fig tree one more year while he digs and manures around it, making delay a chance for fruit.
The commentary's pressure yields either benefit or dry loss; the gardener says future fruit will spare the tree, otherwise it can be cut down, completing the time-limited exception.

The commentary's garden owners plan to keep all produce; in Jesus' vineyard parable the owner sends servants to receive his fruit when harvest time arrives, setting up a precise conflict over what must be handed over.
The commentary's withheld crop brings the holders' loss; the hearers say the owner will destroy the violent tenants and lease the vineyard to others who will deliver fruit in season.

The commentary makes constriction either draw out good fruit or leave a dry loss; Jesus says the vinedresser removes branches without fruit and prunes fruiting ones for more yield, distinguishing two outcomes of cutting.
The commentary's garden is ruined while its keepers sleep and appears lost at daybreak; the disciples see Jesus' fig tree withered to its roots as they pass it in the morning.

row.basis: farmer waits for early and late rain
row.note: The commentary's crop survives a long interval before the year of pressing; James tells readers to be patient like a farmer waiting for precious fruit and early and late rains, tying endurance to delayed yield.

row.basis: rain makes land useful and blessed
row.note: The commentary's pressed cloud starts a chain from water to benefit; Hebrews says land that drinks repeated rain and produces a useful crop receives blessing, then uses that field to describe the hearers' response.
The commentary's destroyed garden is the loss side of a moral agricultural image; Hebrews contrasts land bearing thorns, near a curse and ending in fire, with the rain-fed useful crop just described.
The commentary's late-coming hour can turn protected waiting into missed opportunity; in the bridesmaids' parable the bridegroom is delayed and all fall asleep, setting up the later closed door.
The commentary's shelter can preserve those inside through a span while others lose entry; prepared bridesmaids enter the wedding and the door is shut when the bridegroom comes.

row.basis: unknown day and hour require watchfulness
row.note: The commentary's unnamed asr leaves its exact temporal extent open while the coming judgment matters; Jesus concludes the bridesmaids' scene by telling hearers to watch because they do not know the day or hour.

The commentary's cave shelters believers from hostility across centuries; Revelation shows rulers and others hiding in caves and rocks when judgment arrives, making a cave a place of fear rather than assured rescue.

row.basis: cave dwellers ask rocks to hide them
row.note: The commentary's protected sleepers can leave their cave in mercy; Revelation's terrified people instead ask mountains and rocks to conceal them from the enthroned one, so earthly enclosure cannot promise safety.
The commentary's believers leave their people and find refuge in a cave; Hebrews recalls faithful sufferers wandering deserts, mountains, caves, and holes of earth because of persecution.
The commentary contrasts a hand that retains wealth with one that lets benefit flow; the wealthy are instructed to do good, be rich in works, and be generous and ready to share.
The commentary lets a gift function as lasting provision after ordinary stores fail; the next verse calls sharing a good foundation stored for the future so the givers may take hold of real life.
The commentary's accumulated yield can disappear at the wrong hour; Jesus warns against storing treasure on earth, where moth, corrosion, and thieves destroy or take it.
The commentary's guarded grain and refuge suggest a store that endures; Jesus tells hearers to store treasure in heaven where the stated destroyers and thieves cannot reach it.

row.basis: spend wealth to gain lasting welcome
row.note: The commentary asks whether today's capital yields generosity and shelter later; Jesus says to make friends through worldly wealth so that when it fails they may welcome the giver into enduring dwellings.
The commentary lets the day and a whole life contract toward their end; Paul says the remaining time has been shortened and immediately revises how ordinary attachments are to be held.
The commentary's oath gives force to a later verdict about human loss; the angel proclaims that the hour of God's judgment has come and calls people to fear and worship him.

row.basis: heavens withhold dew after failed harvest
row.note: The commentary's cloud release or closure governs agricultural gain; Haggai says the heavens withheld dew and the earth withheld its produce, supplying the weather side of the pierced-wages lament.
The commentary joins raised storm cloud, rain, and vegetation; Zechariah urges asking the LORD for spring rain and says he makes storm clouds and showers that give plants to every field.
The commentary's stored grain and patience can turn present hardship into eventual yield; the psalm says those sowing in tears will reap with joy, joining time, grain, and reversed loss.

row.basis: fugitive prophet shelters in a cave
row.note: The commentary's youths flee their community into a cave; Elijah reaches a cave and lodges there before hearing the LORD's question, a briefer prophetic refuge without a centuries-long sleep.

row.basis: caves from fear of divine rising
row.note: The commentary's cave opens room for mercy to endangered believers; Isaiah's people enter rock caves and ground holes from the LORD's terror, giving enclosure a contrary meaning at judgment.
The commentary makes the difference between grasping and giving depend on what leaves the hand; Tobit instructs his son to give alms from his property and not turn his face away from the poor.

The commentary's shrinking time remains a place to prepare for what follows; Avot compares this world to a vestibule before the world to come and tells the hearer to prepare there before entering the hall.

The commentary holds a lifetime and a brief final interval together; Avot says one hour of repentance and good deeds in this world exceeds the whole life of the coming world in that respect, placing moral weight on a small unit of time.

The commentary's same grasp can make a giver or a miser; Avot's four property dispositions include treating one's own as another's and another's as another's for the generous case, versus taking both for oneself in the wicked case.

row.basis: master shuts door to late arrivals
row.note: The commentary's time-bound refuge suggests a threshold that can close; Jesus describes a householder shutting the door while people stand outside and ask to be admitted too late.

The commentary's late-day work depends on a finite span of light; Jesus asks whether there are twelve hours in the day and says walking in daylight keeps one from stumbling, elaborating the same time-to-act image as his later saying.

The commentary's delayed relief in Joseph's story and the sleeper's long interval can be heard as purposive waiting; 2 Peter says the Lord is not slow about the promise but patient, giving a specific interpretive bridge for delay.
